name: Remineralising toothpaste

card.summary: Toothpastes with fluoride or mineral agents to repair early enamel damage; fluoride has the strongest evidence.
card.note: Evidence for non-fluoride agents is described as insufficient.

quick.overview:
Remineralising toothpastes aim to restore minerals to early enamel lesions. They use fluoride, nano-hydroxyapatite, calcium phosphate or bioactive glass.

Fluoride has the best evidence; other agents have less.
quick.mechanism: Calcium, phosphate and fluoride are redeposited into enamel weakened by acid.
quick.risks: Excess fluoride is a concern in formulation research; follow label directions.

lead: Remineralising toothpastes are formulated to help redeposit calcium, phosphate or fluoride into demineralised enamel. People use them to strengthen enamel and to help early white spot lesions, the chalky patches left by acid, look less visible, supporting a smoother, healthier-looking smile [1].

Active ingredients include fluoride, nano-hydroxyapatite, amorphous calcium phosphate and bioactive glass [1]. Fluoride has the strongest support, and evidence for bioactive glass and amorphous calcium phosphate is described as insufficient overall [1].

Remineralisation is a natural repair process: acids from plaque bacteria remove mineral, and saliva neutralises them and supplies calcium and phosphate, with fluoride able to form more acid-resistant fluorapatite [1]. A double-blind trial in head and neck radiation patients compared a specially formulated remineralising toothpaste with a conventional fluoride toothpaste for caries control [2].

chain: Toothpaste supplies calcium, phosphate or fluoride
Mineral redeposits in early enamel lesions
Stronger enamel, less visible white spots, healthier-looking teeth
angle.text: The products target early enamel damage that shows as dull or chalky patches and can progress to cavities. Appearance gains come from repairing surface mineral loss, not from changing tooth colour.

infobox: Fluoride, nano-hydroxyapatite, amorphous calcium phosphate, bioactive glass [1]
Developed in Japan in the 1980s, approved there in 1993; European toothpastes in the early 2000s [1]

paras: Fluoride toothpastes use sodium fluoride, sodium monofluorophosphate or stannous fluoride [1]. Nano-hydroxyapatite is a synthetic calcium phosphate nearly identical to tooth mineral, used to fill microfissures [1]. Amorphous calcium phosphate is sold as Recaldent in toothpastes and topical products [1]. Bioactive glass such as Bioglass 45S5 (NovaMin) is calcium sodium phosphosilicate that gives mineral new sites to form and occludes dentin tubules [1]. A self-assembling peptide, P11-4 (Curolox), has been described with remineralisation activity lower than fluoride treatment alone [1]. Research on fluoride-containing bioactive glass for toothpaste notes that excess fluoride is problematic [3].

Fluoride is linked to reduced cavities; evidence for other agents is described as insufficient, with bioactive glass evidence stronger than that for amorphous calcium phosphate but not conclusive [1]. Wikipedia also notes mechanical plaque removal and less frequent sugar exposure support remineralisation [1].
A double-blind randomised trial in head and neck radiation patients compared a dual-phase remineralising toothpaste with a 1100 ppm fluoride dentifrice for caries control [2].

timeline.event: Japan approves nano-hydroxyapatite as an anti-decay agent [1].
A caries trial of a remineralising toothpaste in radiation patients is published [2].
